options.a: Clean and disinfect tools that contacted skin or blood
options.b: Spray tools with disinfectant without first removing the hair
options.c: Place tools in a UV cabinet as the disinfection step
options.d: Disinfect only tools that drew blood, and brush off the rest

distractorExplanations.b: Disinfectant cannot work through hair and debris; tools must be cleaned first, then disinfected for the full contact time.
distractorExplanations.c: UV cabinets are for storing already-disinfected tools; they do not replace an EPA-registered disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.d: Every multi-use tool that touched a client's skin or hair is cleaned and disinfected, not only tools that drew blood.

options.a: Finish the shave first, then apply antiseptic to the nick
options.b: Stop, glove, use antiseptic, and discard contaminated disposables
options.c: Apply a styptic pencil directly and keep it for later clients
options.d: Wipe the blood with the client's towel and continue gloveless

distractorExplanations.a: A blood exposure means stopping the service right away; finishing the shave first spreads exposure and contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Styptic pencils cannot be shared between clients; boards require single-use powder, liquid, or spray styptic.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood exposure protocol requires gloves and discarding contaminated items, not wiping and continuing bare-handed.

options.a: Porous items like buffers and neck strips between clients
options.b: Implements with hair still on them, to save cleaning time
options.c: Nonporous implements after cleaning debris off
options.d: The client's skin before a straight-razor shave

distractorExplanations.a: Porous single-use items like buffers and neck strips are discarded after one client; they cannot be disinfected.
distractorExplanations.b: Disinfectant only works on pre-cleaned surfaces; hair and debris block contact, so cleaning must come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Skin is prepped with an antiseptic, not an EPA disinfectant; disinfectants are for hard, nonporous surfaces.

options.a: Brushed, then disinfected per the label contact time
options.b: Sprayed with clipper disinfectant and used once the mist dries
options.c: Oiled and stored, since blade oil prevents bacterial growth
options.d: Placed in a UV sanitizer, which replaces the disinfectant step

distractorExplanations.b: Using the blade as soon as the mist dries skips the full wet contact time the label requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Blade oil lubricates; it does not disinfect, so the blade still needs cleaning and EPA disinfection.
distractorExplanations.d: UV sanitizers are storage units; they do not meet board requirements for disinfecting implements.

options.a: Serviced with gloves so the open sores are not a concern
options.b: Referred out; do not cut over broken skin
options.c: Serviced after applying antiseptic over the sores
options.d: Serviced if the client signs a liability waiver

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves protect the barber but do not make cutting over open sores safe; the client should be referred to a physician.
distractorExplanations.c: Antiseptic does not make broken skin safe to service; open sores are a reason to decline and refer.
distractorExplanations.d: A waiver does not override board sanitation rules; barbers may not service over open lesions.

options.a: Only after a service that involved visible blood
options.b: At the start and end of each shift, not between clients
options.c: Before service and after any blood or chemical contact
options.d: Before service, with hand sanitizer replacing it after chemicals

distractorExplanations.a: Hands are washed before every service too, not only after visible blood exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: Boards require handwashing before each client, not just at the start and end of the shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand sanitizer does not remove chemical residue; hands are washed with soap and water after chemical contact.

options.a: For the full listed contact time on a pre-cleaned tool
options.b: For a standard one minute, even if hair is still on the tool
options.c: Until the solution air-dries on the tool's surface
options.d: For half the listed time when the solution is freshly mixed

distractorExplanations.b: Contact times vary by product (often 10 minutes) and need a pre-cleaned tool; a fixed one minute is not the rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Air-drying may happen before the label contact time is reached; the surface must stay wet for the full time.
distractorExplanations.d: Fresh solution still needs the full label contact time; mixing date does not shorten it.

options.a: A way to disinfect the blade, since stropping removes bacteria
options.b: Kept clean and not a substitute for disinfection of a soiled blade
options.c: Soaked in disinfectant between clients like a metal implement
options.d: Discarded after each client, like a single-use neck strip

distractorExplanations.a: Stropping only aligns the edge; it does not disinfect, so a soiled blade still needs EPA disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: A leather strop is porous and is not soaked like a metal implement; it is kept clean and used only on a clean razor.
distractorExplanations.d: A strop is a reusable, non-contact tool kept clean, not a single-use item discarded after each client.

options.a: Swept once in the morning before the first client arrives
options.b: Disinfected with spray before the loose hair is swept up
options.c: Swept so hair is not tracked into the next service
options.d: Swept into a corner pile and cleared at closing time

distractorExplanations.a: Hair is swept after each service; a single morning sweep leaves hair from every later client on the floor.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning comes before disinfecting; spraying over loose hair does not work and the hair must be removed first.
distractorExplanations.d: Piling hair in a corner until closing still leaves loose hair in the shop; it is removed after each client.

options.a: Sterilizing implements so that pre-cleaning can be skipped
options.b: Disinfecting combs, brushes, and other plastic tools
options.c: Sanitizing towels and capes between clients
options.d: Sterilizing approved metal implements after cleaning

distractorExplanations.a: Sterilization still requires cleaning first; debris shields microbes from steam.
distractorExplanations.b: Most plastic combs and brushes cannot withstand autoclave heat; they are cleaned and disinfected in solution.
distractorExplanations.c: Towels and capes are laundered; an autoclave is for heat-safe metal implements.

options.a: Replace it; do not guess the concentration
options.b: Top it up with fresh concentrate to restore its strength
options.c: Keep using it until the end of the day, then change it
options.d: Use it for pre-cleaning only, not for disinfecting

distractorExplanations.b: Adding concentrate to spent solution gives an unknown dilution; contaminated solution is discarded and remixed.
distractorExplanations.c: Cloudy or contaminated disinfectant must be changed right away, not at the end of the day.
distractorExplanations.d: Spent disinfectant is discarded; pre-cleaning uses soap and water, not old disinfectant.

options.a: The official NIC barber written exam in practice form
options.b: A licensed copy of a state board's retired exam paper
options.c: An independent diagnostic — not a state board written exam
options.d: The state's required practical exam, offered online

distractorExplanations.a: NIC exams are confidential and administered by testing vendors; UniPrep's mock is independent, not an NIC form.
distractorExplanations.b: UniPrep has no license to state board exam papers; this is an independent diagnostic written from public outlines.
distractorExplanations.d: Practical exams are hands-on and given in person; this is an independent written-style diagnostic.

options.a: Using one guard length all around for an even finish
options.b: Cutting a hard line at one level, then shaving below it
options.c: Removing weight with thinning shears from the crown down
options.d: Blending clipper lengths from short to long with no shelf

distractorExplanations.a: One guard length all around is a buzz cut; a taper fade graduates several lengths.
distractorExplanations.b: A hard line with shaved hair below is an undercut or disconnection; a fade blends with no line.
distractorExplanations.c: Thinning shears remove bulk; a taper fade is built with graduated clipper lengths.

options.a: Remove bulk and blend without a hard line
options.b: Create a sharp outline at the hairline and nape
options.c: Cut a disconnected undercut with a visible line
options.d: Add texture to the ends by point cutting

distractorExplanations.b: Sharp outlines are made with a trimmer or razor; clipper-over-comb removes bulk and blends.
distractorExplanations.c: A disconnected undercut leaves a visible line, the opposite of the blend clipper-over-comb creates.
distractorExplanations.d: Point cutting with shears adds texture; clipper-over-comb removes bulk and blends.

options.a: Remove all the hair in one pass
options.b: Reduce irritation before a closer pass
options.c: Lift the hair so the razor can cut against it
options.d: Replace the need for a pre-shave hot towel

distractorExplanations.a: The first pass with the grain is not meant to finish the shave; a closer second pass may follow.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting against the grain is the later, closer pass; the first pass goes with the grain to limit irritation.
distractorExplanations.d: The hot towel softens the beard before any razor pass; the first-pass direction does not replace it.

options.a: Cut straight across at the natural hairline in every style
options.b: Set high above the natural hairline so it grows out slower
options.c: Crisp, even, and appropriate to the agreed style
options.d: Blocked square on every client for a sharper look

distractorExplanations.a: Neckline shape (blocked, rounded, tapered) depends on the agreed style, not one straight line for all.
distractorExplanations.b: Setting the line too high above the natural hairline makes regrowth show sooner, not slower.
distractorExplanations.d: A blocked neckline suits some styles, but the shape should match the client's agreed style.

options.a: Creating a skin-tight fade line at the sides
options.b: Edging a sharp outline around the ears
options.c: Blending the nape to the skin with a foil shaver
options.d: Soft texture and length control

distractorExplanations.a: Skin fades on the sides are clipper and shaver work; shear-over-comb shapes longer hair on top.
distractorExplanations.b: Edging around the ears is trimmer or razor work, not shear-over-comb.
distractorExplanations.c: Foil shavers finish skin fades at the nape; shear-over-comb controls length and texture on top.

options.a: Looking at the cut from another angle or section to catch holes
options.b: Recutting each section a second time at the same elevation and angle
options.c: Checking that guard numbers match the client's last visit
options.d: Comparing the finished cut to the client's reference photo

distractorExplanations.b: Cross-checking uses the opposite sectioning direction to find holes; recutting the same way repeats errors.
distractorExplanations.c: Matching guard numbers to the last visit is consultation, not cross-checking the finished cut.
distractorExplanations.d: Comparing to a photo checks style agreement; cross-checking inspects the cut from another angle to catch holes.

options.a: Using a guard that is too long for the fade
options.b: A blade too aggressive or a dry, rushed pass
options.c: Lathering the skin before using the foil shaver
options.d: Cutting with the grain on the first pass

distractorExplanations.a: A guard that is too long leaves hair longer; nicks come from bare blades used aggressively.
distractorExplanations.c: Lubricated or prepped skin reduces nicks; a dry, rushed pass causes them.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting with the grain first lowers irritation; nicks come from aggressive or rushed passes.

options.a: Sit as high on the cheek as the hair grows for fullness
options.b: Follow the same line on every client for consistency
options.c: Follow bone structure and the client's requested line
options.d: Be set by the barber's taste rather than the client's

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the natural high cheek growth ignores the agreed design and the client's bone structure.
distractorExplanations.b: One standard line ignores each client's face shape and requested design.
distractorExplanations.d: The client decides the beard line; the barber advises but does not impose a design.

options.a: Cutting a blunt perimeter line on the nape
options.b: Shortening overall length in one quick pass
options.c: Blending a skin fade at the temple
options.d: Removing bulk without losing the outline

distractorExplanations.a: Blunt perimeter lines are cut with regular shears or clippers; thinning shears remove bulk inside the shape.
distractorExplanations.b: Thinning shears remove a fraction of hair per cut; they do not shorten overall length quickly.
distractorExplanations.c: Skin fades are blended with clippers and shavers; thinning shears remove bulk in longer hair.

options.a: Softening hair and skin before the razor
options.b: Closing the pores before lather goes on
options.c: Disinfecting the skin so antiseptic can be skipped
options.d: Reusing the towel for the next client once rewarmed

distractorExplanations.b: A hot towel opens and softens; a cool towel after the shave is the closing step.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat does not disinfect skin; a hot towel only softens the beard before shaving.
distractorExplanations.d: Towels are single-use per client and must be laundered; rewarming does not clean them.

options.a: Combing a natural part with styling product to hold it
options.b: Blending the part area with a #1 guard to soften it
options.c: Cutting or shaving a clean part line the client asked for
options.d: Shaving the part line to match the barber's preference

distractorExplanations.a: A combed part with product is a soft part; a hard part is a cut or shaved line.
distractorExplanations.b: Blending with a guard softens the area, the opposite of the clean line that makes a hard part.
distractorExplanations.d: A hard part's placement is agreed with the client; it is not set by the barber's preference.

options.a: Blending the beard with clipper-over-comb technique
options.b: Checking with the client how low to take the fade
options.c: Using guards in gradual steps up into the beard
options.d: A dark shelf where the beard meets the cheek fade

distractorExplanations.a: Clipper-over-comb is a standard blending method; the thing to avoid is a dark shelf at the join.
distractorExplanations.b: Confirming fade height with the client is good consultation practice, not something to avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Gradual guard steps create the blend; skipping them causes the shelf you want to avoid.

options.a: Cutting with the growth pattern, not against it blindly
options.b: Cutting the crown extra short so the cowlick lies flat
options.c: Cutting against the growth to train the hair down
options.d: Thinning the crown heavily to remove the swirl

distractorExplanations.b: Cutting a cowlick very short often makes it stand up more; leaving weight helps it lie down.
distractorExplanations.c: Hair cannot be trained by cutting against the growth; it springs up and leaves holes.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy thinning removes the weight that holds the cowlick down, making it stick up more.

options.a: Follow each side's natural hairline even if uneven
options.b: Match both sides and the agreed tightness
options.c: Push the line back on every client to look sharper
options.d: Be cut freehand without checking in the mirror

distractorExplanations.a: Temple outlines are balanced on both sides; following an uneven hairline leaves the cut lopsided.
distractorExplanations.c: Pushing the line back is a common error that recedes the hairline; follow the agreed tightness.
distractorExplanations.d: Outlines are checked in the mirror for symmetry; freehand without checking risks uneven sides.

options.a: Left on until the timer ends, then neutralized as usual
options.b: Covered with base cream and processed a few more minutes
options.c: Neutralized on the spot without rinsing the cream out
options.d: Rinsed immediately per the manufacturer's emergency steps

distractorExplanations.a: Burning means a chemical injury is starting; waiting for the timer worsens it, so rinse at once.
distractorExplanations.b: Base cream is applied before the relaxer; it cannot stop a burn, and more processing worsens it.
distractorExplanations.c: Neutralizing before rinsing traps relaxer on the scalp; a thorough rinse comes first.

options.a: Oxidative color or bleach systems as labeled
options.b: Disinfecting implements between clients
options.c: Cleaning a nick before applying a styptic
options.d: Pre-softening coarse beard hair before a shave

distractorExplanations.b: Developer is not an EPA-registered disinfectant; implements need a registered disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.c: Developer is far stronger than first-aid peroxide and is not for wounds; use an antiseptic.
distractorExplanations.d: Beards are softened with hot towels and lather; developer is a color oxidizer.

options.a: Scalp haircolor works the same on beard hair and skin
options.b: Skin staining and allergy risk — follow the beard-color directions
options.c: Higher-volume developer gives better gray coverage on beards
options.d: A patch test is unnecessary for products made for beards

distractorExplanations.a: Facial skin is more sensitive and stains easily; use products labeled for beards.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher-volume developer raises irritation risk on facial skin; follow the beard product's directions.
distractorExplanations.d: Beard dyes can contain the same allergens as scalp color; follow the label's patch-test directions.

options.a: Restore the hair's pH by rinsing with plain water
options.b: Soften the hair further before the final smoothing
options.c: Stop the straightening process and rebuild bonds as directed
options.d: Break the remaining disulfide bonds for a straighter result

distractorExplanations.a: Rinsing removes relaxer, but bonds re-form only with the oxidizing neutralizer.
distractorExplanations.b: Neutralizer stops processing; further softening is what the relaxer did, not the neutralizer.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaking disulfide bonds is the thio relaxer's job; the neutralizer re-forms them.

options.a: Allowed after a negative patch test 24 hours earlier
options.b: Safe when applied with a protective petroleum barrier
options.c: Permitted on brows since they sit farther from the eye
options.d: Prohibited in most shops — not a barber brow service

distractorExplanations.a: A patch test does not make aniline tint legal near the eyes; the FDA bans it on lashes and brows.
distractorExplanations.b: A petroleum barrier does not make aniline tint safe near the eye; blindness risk remains.
distractorExplanations.c: The FDA restriction covers brows as well as lashes; distance from the eye does not make it permitted.

options.a: After the time the manufacturer specifies, often 24–48 hours
options.b: After 15 minutes, before the client leaves the chair
options.c: After one week, to catch delayed reactions
options.d: Right before applying color, about an hour after placement

distractorExplanations.b: Allergic contact reactions take hours to appear; a 15-minute read is too early to show them.
distractorExplanations.c: Labels set 24–48 hours; waiting a week is not the manufacturer's read time.
distractorExplanations.d: One hour is too soon for a delayed reaction; most labels call for 24–48 hours.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Allergy tests need time. This item asks: “A patch test is typically read:”. The matching answer is: After the time the manufacturer and board specify, often 24–48 hours. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official state barber board paper. Some state boards set their own read time as well.

options.a: Acceptable if both relaxers are the same base type
options.b: Outside the label — a chemical injury risk
options.c: Acceptable for coarse, resistant hair after a strand test
options.d: Acceptable if the mixture is timed for half as long

distractorExplanations.a: Same base type does not make mixing safe; formulas differ and the result is untested.
distractorExplanations.c: Resistant hair needs a stronger single product as labeled, not a homemade mixture.
distractorExplanations.d: Shorter timing does not make an untested caustic mixture safe for the scalp.

options.a: Shaved closely as usual, since minoxidil affects only hair
options.b: Shaved against the grain to remove the extra growth
options.c: Refused service until the client stops the medication
options.d: Asked about skin sensitivity; shave gently or defer if inflamed

distractorExplanations.a: Topical minoxidil can irritate and dry skin; ask about sensitivity before a close shave.
distractorExplanations.b: Against-the-grain shaving raises irritation risk on sensitive, medicated skin.
distractorExplanations.c: Minoxidil alone is no reason to refuse; adjust the shave or defer if the skin is inflamed.

options.a: Sting and delay clotting — treat the nick first
options.b: Disinfect the nick in place of a proper antiseptic
options.c: Close the cut faster than a styptic powder
options.d: Seal the skin so gloves are not needed

distractorExplanations.b: Aftershave is a cosmetic, not an approved antiseptic for wound care.
distractorExplanations.c: Styptic is the product that stops bleeding; aftershave on a fresh nick mainly stings.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are required when handling a blood exposure; aftershave seals nothing.

options.a: A same-day corrective relaxer to even out the texture
options.b: A gentle reconstructive plan, not more chemical
options.c: A thermal straightening set to smooth the damaged ends
options.d: A bleach bath to remove buildup before conditioning

distractorExplanations.a: Another chemical on overprocessed hair causes breakage; correction waits for recovery.
distractorExplanations.c: High heat on overprocessed hair causes more breakage; it needs gentle reconditioning first.
distractorExplanations.d: Bleach is a harsh chemical that worsens overprocessed hair; reconditioning comes first.

options.a: Showing clients the product's retail ingredient list
options.b: Recording the date each disinfectant jar is changed
options.c: Looking up first aid and handling for a product
options.d: Documenting client allergies before chemical services

distractorExplanations.a: SDS are for safety data such as hazards, first aid, and handling, not retail ingredient lists.
distractorExplanations.b: Jar-change dates go in a disinfection log; SDS give hazard and first-aid data.
distractorExplanations.d: Client allergies go on the client record card; SDS describe product hazards.

options.a: The client from bacteria on the barber's hands
options.b: The product from contamination by skin oils
options.c: The barber's hands from cuts by sharp implements
options.d: The barber's skin from repeated chemical exposure

distractorExplanations.a: During chemical services gloves mainly protect the barber from the chemical, not the client from bacteria.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are PPE for the barber; preventing product contamination is not their purpose here.
distractorExplanations.c: Disposable gloves do not stop cuts; they guard against chemical contact dermatitis.

options.a: Stain skin and trigger allergy — treat it as a chemical
options.b: Be applied safely without a patch test since it is plant-based
options.c: Wash out fully after a few shampoos like a color rinse
options.d: Be layered over oxidative tint without any reaction

distractorExplanations.b: 'Natural' does not mean allergy-free; follow the label's patch-test directions for henna too.
distractorExplanations.c: Henna is long-lasting and does not wash out like a temporary color rinse.
distractorExplanations.d: Compound hennas with metallic salts can react with oxidative products and damage hair.

options.a: Kept at home and shown to inspectors on request
options.b: Current and displayed as the board requires
options.c: Renewed only when the shop changes owners
options.d: Valid in any state once issued by one board

distractorExplanations.a: Most boards require the license to be posted at the work station, not kept at home.
distractorExplanations.c: Licenses are renewed on the board's cycle, not when the shop changes owners.
distractorExplanations.d: Licenses are state-specific; working elsewhere needs reciprocity or endorsement.

options.a: Sweep hair and clean the shop floor
options.b: Book appointments and handle payments
options.c: Perform paid haircuts or shaves
options.d: Launder towels and restock retail shelves

distractorExplanations.a: Sweeping and cleaning are not barbering services, so unlicensed staff may do them.
distractorExplanations.b: Reception and payment tasks are not licensed services; unlicensed staff may do them.
distractorExplanations.d: Laundry and stocking are support tasks that do not require a barber license.

options.a: Only the service price and the client's phone number
options.b: The client's medical diagnoses as reported by their physician
options.c: The product brand, with timing and results left to memory
options.d: Date, service, and any test or incident notes the board expects

distractorExplanations.a: Price and phone are not enough; records note the service, tests, and any incident.
distractorExplanations.b: Barbers do not collect physician diagnoses; records note service, tests, and incidents.
distractorExplanations.c: Timing and results must be written down; memory is not a record the board accepts.

options.a: A parent/guardian as state law requires for services or photos
options.b: Written consent from the minor alone once they are over the age of 12
options.c: A licensed cosmetologist rather than a barber
options.d: No consent for a haircut, only for chemical services

distractorExplanations.b: Minors generally cannot give legal consent on their own; a parent or guardian consents.
distractorExplanations.c: Barbers may serve minors; the issue is guardian consent, not license type.
distractorExplanations.d: Guardian consent rules can apply to services and photos, not only chemicals.

options.a: Allowed if the barber completed a trichology course
options.b: Prohibited misleading advertising
options.c: Allowed if a physician works in the same building
options.d: A sanitation violation handled by the health department

distractorExplanations.a: A trichology course does not make someone an MD; the claim is still misleading.
distractorExplanations.c: A nearby physician does not let a barber claim to be one; it is still false advertising.
distractorExplanations.d: It is a false-advertising and scope violation, not a sanitation matter.

options.a: A warning only, since boards cannot fine a shop
options.b: Penalties for the owner but not for licensed staff
options.c: Fines or closure for sanitation or licensing failures
options.d: Citations for sanitation issues, not for license status

distractorExplanations.a: Boards can fine, suspend, or close shops; inspections are not warning-only.
distractorExplanations.b: Individual licensees can be cited for their own violations, not just owners.
distractorExplanations.d: Inspectors check licenses too; expired or missing licenses lead to citations.

options.a: Optional for experienced barbers
options.b: Required only for instructors
options.c: Needed to reinstate a lapsed license
options.d: Needed to renew on time

distractorExplanations.a: Where CE is required, experience does not exempt a barber; it is a renewal condition.
distractorExplanations.b: Where states require CE, it applies to licensed barbers, not just instructors.
distractorExplanations.c: CE is a routine renewal requirement, not only a reinstatement step after a lapse.

options.a: Unlawful discrimination
options.b: Allowed if the shop posts a refusal policy
options.c: A matter for the shop owner's discretion
options.d: Allowed in a private booth-rental space

distractorExplanations.b: A posted policy does not override public-accommodation law banning race discrimination.
distractorExplanations.c: Race discrimination is illegal; owner discretion does not extend to protected classes.
distractorExplanations.d: Booth renters serve the public and are bound by the same anti-discrimination law.

options.a: Covered by the shop owner's license for sanitation
options.b: Responsible for their license and station sanitation
options.c: Exempt from inspections at their rented chair
options.d: Free to set sanitation rules apart from the board's

distractorExplanations.a: Booth renters are responsible for their own station; the owner's license does not cover them.
distractorExplanations.c: Rented stations are inspected like any other; renting does not exempt them.
distractorExplanations.d: Board sanitation rules apply to every licensee; renters cannot set their own.

options.a: Offer the shave under a supervising barber's endorsement
options.b: Offer the shave if the client signs a consent form
options.c: Get the endorsement or do not offer that shave
options.d: Offer the shave using a disposable-blade razor instead

distractorExplanations.a: Endorsements are personal; working under someone else's does not authorize you.
distractorExplanations.b: Client consent does not replace a required state endorsement.
distractorExplanations.d: A disposable-blade straight razor is still a straight razor under the endorsement rule.

options.a: A voluntary gratuity line on the client's receipt
options.b: Part of the cash wage where a tip credit legally applies
options.c: The optional extra a client hands a booth renter
options.d: Sales tax or shop policies on reporting, where they apply

distractorExplanations.a: A gratuity line is where a tip is recorded, so tips do fill it; tax and reporting duties remain.
distractorExplanations.b: Under federal tip-credit rules tips can count toward part of a tipped worker's wage.
distractorExplanations.c: That extra cash is itself a tip; it still has to be reported as income.

options.a: Consent — especially for faces of minors
options.b: Consent only if the face shows
options.c: No consent if the photo is posted on the shop's page
options.d: Consent from the shop owner, not the client

distractorExplanations.b: Identifiable features such as tattoos can identify a client too; ask consent for any client photo.
distractorExplanations.c: Posting on the shop's own page is still public use of a likeness and needs consent.
distractorExplanations.d: The likeness belongs to the client; the owner cannot consent for them.

options.a: Only the unlicensed coworker can face a board penalty for the violation
options.b: You can be pulled into a shop violation — report per board rules
options.c: It is allowed if they cut under your supervision
options.d: It is the shop owner's problem to handle, not yours to report to the board

distractorExplanations.a: Licensees and owners who aid unlicensed practice can also be disciplined.
distractorExplanations.c: Supervision does not license a coworker unless they are a registered apprentice in a program.
distractorExplanations.d: Licensees can share liability; the board expects violations to be reported.

options.a: A license, with sanitation rules waived off-site
options.b: Only the event host's permit to cover the barber
options.c: A license and sanitation you can prove

distractorExplanations.a: Sanitation rules apply wherever the service is performed, including events.
distractorExplanations.b: The host's permit does not replace the barber's own license.
distractorExplanations.d: Boards generally require the license to be available where services are provided.

options.a: Leaving implements soaking in the disinfectant jar overnight to save time
options.b: Storing used and disinfected implements in one drawer

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving implements in solution overnight exceeds the contact time and damages tools; remove, dry, and store.
distractorExplanations.b: Used and disinfected implements must be kept apart to prevent cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemicals must be closed and stored at closing to prevent spills and exposure.
